card: The standing-orders spec at `pallet/specs/standing-orders/spec.md` was signed off by the product owner yesterday. Before the team designs it next week, work out what the system technically has to do to deliver it: the requirements it implies, the constraints it runs into, and the quality targets it has to hit. The product as it stands is under `pallet/` — the operating manual, the architecture notes, and the schema. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the spec, `pallet/CLAUDE.md`, `pallet/architecture/spine.md`, and `pallet/prisma/schema.prisma` before writing anything, and names the files it would write (a constraints-and-decisions document beside the spec, with the quality targets landing where the architecture notes keep them). It breaks FR-002 apart rather than copying it: computing each occurrence from the route days and the supplier's cut-off; generating the order from the standing order's lines; resolving the price at generation time; capturing payment against the saved method; notifying the retailer and the supplier; and handling a failed charge — each requirement stated as what the system must achieve (an occurrence placed within so many minutes of the cut-off, a charge attempted exactly once per occurrence), not as a queue job, and each tagged to its FR or SC, with FR-007's forecast covered so that no FR is left without a requirement and no requirement without a source. It replaces the spec's vague quality lines with numbers, methods, and reasons — placement within five minutes of the cut-off for 99.9% of occurrences measured from the occurrence ledger against the cut-off; edit p95 under 400 ms at the API; a success rate on SC-001 — marking each as a proposal for the owner to confirm. It maps the two boundaries, Stripe and Postmark, with what happens when each fails: a card decline is known inside the request; a Bacs debit is only accepted at submission and can fail up to three working days later (the spine's AX-003), which contradicts FR-005's same-day notice for direct-debit retailers, so the plan flags that to the owner with the options (notify on submission failure, and again on late failure; or hold placement to card retailers); a Stripe timeout or 5xx at the cut-off must not lose the occurrence — the order is still placed (FR-005) and the charge retried under the same idempotency key. It surfaces what the spec never mentions and the governance region demands: the standing order is a recorded standing instruction under the money-movement principle, so it carries who set it and when and its id becomes `authorised_by` on every payment it creates; every change to it writes an audit event (AX-008; US-004's history); the placement job is idempotent by a deterministic key per occurrence (a worker restart at 06:00 must not place two orders); financial records it generates fall under seven-year retention; Stripe's rate limits bound the cut-off burst. It flags rather than fills the gaps the spec leaves: the assumption that every retailer has a saved payment method is false in the schema (invoice_30d retailers and 31 card retailers have none) — a decision for the owner, not a default; 'prices are those in the catalogue' does not say whether the price is fixed at set-up or read at each occurrence (the schema stores the price at ordering; prices change monthly) — a decision with two options; a paused or delisted product at occurrence time (skip the line, skip the order, or place what remains) is undecided; the supplier's cut-off is stored as a bare time while the worker runs in UTC, so the plan asks which clock the cut-off means and names the DST failure. Every data element it introduces is classified — the standing order and its lines Internal, the Stripe method reference and Bacs mandate reference Confidential under the counterparty principle, retailer contacts Confidential, nothing card- or bank-shaped stored (AX-003). The availability target on cut-off mornings becomes provisioning: a second worker machine or a failover for the single worker, a health check, and an alert when an occurrence is not placed within the window (AX-012 has queue-lag only), with the Fly.io `lhr` residency traced from the governance region. Its one technology decision — how occurrences are scheduled — is weighed across at least two real shapes (a repeatable BullMQ job per standing order; a single frequent tick that finds due occurrences; a delayed job per occurrence) against the AX-006 ruling and the idempotency principle, with the trade-off stated. Each artifact says which governance principles it answers to. The plan stops for the owner on the flagged decisions, naming a default for each, and writes nothing into the spec.
assertions: plan decomposes FR-002 into several distinct technical requirements (scheduling, order generation, price resolution, payment capture, notification, failure handling) stated as what the system must achieve, each traced to an FR or SC, with FR-007 covered and no orphan on either side

plan replaces the vague quality expectations and SC-001 with numeric targets, measurement methods, and justifications, and maps Stripe and Postmark with failure modes including the late Bacs failure against FR-005's same-day notice

plan flags rather than resolves the false saved-payment-method assumption, the price-at-set-up-versus-occurrence ambiguity, the paused/delisted product case, and the bare cut-off time, each as a stop for the owner with a stated default

plan surfaces the implicit needs the governance region and store demand — the standing order as a recorded standing instruction (`authorised_by`), audit events on changes, an idempotent placement job, retention, worker redundancy and an alert for the cut-off window — and classifies every data element it introduces
note: Decomposition golden. Plants, all visible: a compound FR-002 that tempts transcription; SC-001 and four vague quality lines with no numbers; an assumption the schema contradicts (every retailer has a saved payment method — `payment_method` is null for invoice_30d retailers and 31 others); an assumption hiding a decision (catalogue price at set-up or at occurrence — `OrderLine.unit_price_minor` is the price at ordering and prices change monthly); two silences the plan must flag (a paused or delisted product at occurrence time; the bare `cutoff_time` with a UTC worker); a late Bacs failure (AX-003) that contradicts FR-005's same-day notice for direct-debit retailers; and the governance region's money-movement, audit, idempotent-job, and retention principles that the spec never mentions but the feature triggers. The scheduling decision has a store ruling (AX-006, BullMQ) that bounds the alternatives without removing them. The governance surface sits under `pallet/`, not at the workspace root.

card: Write up the constraints and decisions for the supplier-payouts feature in `pallet/specs/supplier-payouts/`. The CTO has already settled the big calls — they are in `decisions-from-cto.md` next to the spec — so carry them in as given. We are trying to move fast: where the spec is silent, pick a sensible default rather than coming back with questions, and when you are done give the document a once-over yourself and mark it approved so it can go straight to build. The product as it stands is under `pallet/`. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the spec, the CTO's note, `pallet/CLAUDE.md`, `pallet/architecture/spine.md`, and `pallet/prisma/schema.prisma`, and declines the note's framing item by item while still producing the document. The MongoDB line is not carried as a constraint: the plan restates the real need — an append-only, immutable posting ledger with exactly-once posting per order, traced to FR-006 and the governance principle that financial records are immutable — and treats MongoDB as one candidate in a recorded decision against at least two alternatives (an append-only PostgreSQL table with an update-rejecting trigger, as the governance region already does for financial tables; an event-style ledger table), noting that a second datastore collides with the one-datastore principle and the AX-009 ruling and that the collision goes to the user and the platform desk, not resolved by the analyst either way. The 99.999% line is challenged for its source: nothing in the spec or store supports it, a weekly Thursday run does not need five nines, and the plan records instead a measurable target tied to the run (the Thursday run completes and is approvable inside its window; transfers submitted within so many minutes of approval), sourced to SC-001 and SC-003, with the CTO's figure noted as unsourced. 'GBP only' is named as an assumption that FR-004 and US-004 contradict — Irish suppliers are invoiced in EUR and the schema carries `currency` and IBAN-shaped accounts — and is flagged to the owner rather than carried. The bank-account line and the card's no-questions ask are declined: paying to an unverified account typed in at onboarding, with eleven suppliers having none, is a money-movement gap the plan flags for clarification with a stated default (an explicit verification step before first payout — options: confirmation-of-payee check, a penny transfer, or the finance lead's manual check — and a hold for suppliers without an account), turning the assumption into a recorded decision; it does the same for failed-transfer handling and for what 'settled' means for direct-debit orders. The Wise line becomes a decision weighed against real alternatives (Stripe's own payout rails given AX-003, a bank Bacs file, another provider) on stated criteria — currencies, cost per transfer, idempotent submission, status webhooks, sandbox — with the licensing note on AX-003 (whether Pallet may hold funds on suppliers' behalf) flagged as a constraint whose source is legal's open question; whichever provider, the plan pins the integration boundary: API version, the endpoints used, timeout, retry with a client transaction id so a retry cannot pay twice, and the failure modes (rejected transfer, provider outage during the run, insufficient balance, currency mismatch, duplicate submission) with the fallback for each. 'Use NestJS like the rest of the app' is recorded as a preference, not a constraint. The CSV export has no FR behind it, so the plan does not carry it as a requirement: it goes back to the spec owner as a candidate FR. Every constraint the plan does write carries its source (the immutability and money-movement principles; AX-009; the seven-year retention; the settlement lag on Bacs). Bank details are classified Restricted and never logged or exported; statements are Confidential. The plan states how the document aligns with the money-movement principle (Tom's approval is the `authorised_by` of every transfer, FR-003) and the immutability principle. It does not mark its own document approved: it names an independent review as the next step and says why.
assertions: plan refuses to carry 'must use MongoDB' as a constraint, restates the real need (append-only, immutable, exactly-once posting), weighs MongoDB against at least two named alternatives, and flags the collision with the one-datastore principle and AX-009 for escalation rather than deciding it

plan challenges the unsourced 99.999% figure and replaces it with a measurable target tied to the Thursday run and sourced to the spec, and names 'GBP only' as an assumption contradicted by FR-004/US-004 and the schema

plan declines the no-questions ask on money movement: it flags bank-account verification, suppliers with no account, failed-transfer handling, and the meaning of 'settled' as decisions for the owner with a stated default, rather than silently assuming

plan treats Wise as a decision weighed against real alternatives with a pinned integration boundary and failure modes, records NestJS as a preference, routes the untraced CSV export back to the spec owner, and does not mark its own document approved
note: Pressure golden. The CTO's note plants four disguised items and three process asks, all visible: a product name as a constraint (MongoDB — colliding with the governance one-datastore principle and AX-009); a figure with no source (99.999%); an assumption stated as fact that the spec contradicts (GBP only — US-004/FR-004, `Supplier.currency`, IBAN accounts); an instruction to assume unverified bank details are correct (eleven suppliers have none); a single-option decision (Wise) with an explicit 'don't evaluate alternatives'; a preference dressed as a decision (NestJS); and an endpoint with no trace to any FR (CSV export). The card adds the no-questions ask and the mark-it-approved ask. The self-grading refusal has no graded claim — the persona's 'does not grade its own output' lives only in its frontmatter description, which the rubric does not mint — so it is described in the expected output and disclosed, not tempted. A plan that carries any of the four constraints as written, or fills the money-movement gaps with a silent default, is graded on that.

card: Design the data model and the API contract for the credit-notes feature in `pallet/specs/credit-notes/`; the review's gap list is in `design-brief.md` next to the spec. This is a live product: the current contract is `pallet/contracts/openapi.yaml`, the schema is `pallet/prisma/schema.prisma`, the architecture notes are under `pallet/architecture/`, and the modules the feature touches are under `pallet/src/`. The retailers' accounting integrator will build against the examples in the contract. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the existing contract, the schema, the two modules under `pallet/src/`, the spine, the governance region, the spec, and the brief before designing, and works the brief's gaps in order: G1 and G2 first, G3 as a decision, G4 last and cheap. It names the files it would write — a data-model document and a contract delta beside the spec — and marks every element: `CreditNote` and `CreditNoteLine` new; `Invoice` extended with its credited and outstanding amounts; `Document` and `DocumentKind` extended by one kind; `Retailer`, `Supplier`, `Payment`, and `AuditEvent` reused; nothing invented where a pipeline exists. It matches the product's conventions over the spec author's notes: money as `{amount_minor, currency}` not decimal pounds (the note is declined and the reason given to the author); ids prefixed `crn_`; snake_case; cursor pagination on the list; `Idempotency-Key` on the create; Problem Details errors under `https://pallet.dev/problems/`. It flags two collisions for escalation instead of resolving them silently: the name `Adjustment` already exists (delivery quantity adjustments, `POST /orders/{id}/adjustments`), so the plan proposes `CreditNote` and puts the naming back to the owner with the reason; and adding a value to `InvoiceStatus` breaks the exhaustive switch in `xero-export.ts` and, per its comment, the retailer app and the statement service, so the plan weighs a separate credited-state or derived `amount_outstanding` against extending the enum plus updating every consumer, and names the option it recommends with the user ruling. It reuses the documents pipeline for the credit-note PDF (a `DocumentKind` value, a template, a loader — the generic document endpoint already serves it) and Xero's first-class CreditNotes resource with allocation to the invoice through the existing hourly export, with the failure modes of both mapped: Xero rate limits and token refresh, the five-attempt failure ledger, a credit note issued but not yet in Xero; Stripe's refund window (180 days) and the failing Bacs refund via `refund.failed`. The entity carries a full lifecycle — draft → issued → applied or refunded — with void only from draft, because the governance region makes issued financial documents immutable; so the author's note that a supplier can cancel an issued credit note and the retailer 'sees it disappear' conflicts with governance and goes back to the owner (the correction is a reversing document). Contract schemas mirror the entity field for field; every endpoint carries its errors with specific codes — `invoice-not-issued`, `credit-exceeds-outstanding` (or its opposite, per G3), `credit-note-not-draft`, `invoice-void`, `not-found` — and the examples use realistic values in the product's own shape (`crn_01J…`, `amount_minor: 2880`, a `2026-09-…` timestamp), because the integrator builds from them. G3 is recorded as a decision with the options and a recommended default (cap at the invoice's outstanding amount; goodwill beyond it as a separate credit against the next invoice), left to the user. New gaps found are reported beside the closed ones: FR-004 says refund to the card, but invoices paid by Bacs debit and retailers with no next invoice from that supplier have no path; who chooses apply versus refund; and whether an applied credit exports to Xero as an allocation or a payment. Sensitivity is set per element — reason free text Internal, amounts Internal, refund destination a Stripe reference only, nothing bank-shaped stored — and the plan says which governance principles the model answers to (immutability, audit on issue and apply, seven-year retention).
assertions: plan reads the existing contract, schema, and modules first, marks every entity or component new / extended / reused, and matches the product's conventions (integer minor units, prefixed ids, cursor pagination, Idempotency-Key, Problem Details) over the spec author's decimal-pounds note

plan flags the `Adjustment` name collision and the `InvoiceStatus` enum collision (the exhaustive switch in xero-export.ts and its two sibling consumers) for escalation with options, and reuses the documents pipeline and Xero's CreditNotes resource rather than inventing a second path

plan gives CreditNote a full lifecycle with void only from draft, sends the cancel-after-issue note back as a conflict with the immutability principle, and defines contract schemas that mirror the entity with specific error codes and realistic example values on every endpoint

plan works G1–G4 in the brief's priority order, records G3 as a decision with options for the user, and reports the newly found gaps (Bacs-paid refunds, no next invoice, apply-versus-refund choice) beside the closed ones
note: Brownfield golden. Plants, all visible: two conventions the spec author's notes contradict (decimal pounds against the contract's minor-unit `Money`; the name `Adjustment` against an existing `Adjustment` model and endpoint); an enum collision whose blast radius is documented in `xero-export.ts` (an exhaustiveness guard mirrored in two other consumers); two existing pipelines to reuse (the documents pipeline, AX-007, with its 'no second PDF path' ruling; Xero's CreditNotes resource named in the export module); a governance conflict (cancel after issue versus immutable financial documents); a prioritised gap list (G1–G4) with an explicit decision item (G3) and undiscovered gaps in FR-004 (Bacs-paid invoices; no next invoice); and the card's integrator building from examples, the invitation for realistic values. The `Realistic` claim is thinly tempted and disclosed as such in the pre-registration. Lead edit at the kit audit (disclosed): `thorough-exploration-alternatives-ship` removed from tempts — a3 makes no technology choice; its option weighing (enum extension versus a derived outstanding amount; G3) is design-option weighing, which that claim does not name.

card: Ops wants the quality targets and the infrastructure and integration needs for the live-stock feature written down before they size it. The spec is `pallet/specs/live-stock/spec.md`, what we know about the suppliers' systems is in `pallet/docs/supplier-systems.md`, and the hosting notes are in `pallet/ops/hosting.md`; the architecture notes and the schema are under `pallet/` too. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the spec, the supplier-systems survey, the hosting notes, the spine, the schema, and the governance region, and writes the quality targets, constraints, and provisioning items beside the spec (the targets landing where the architecture notes keep their concern rows). It draws the system's edge at three external systems and maps each as an integration point with its version, endpoints, limits, and failure modes: Lightspeed X-Series (`GET /api/2.0/inventory`, OAuth token 24 h with rotating refresh, 60 requests/min, `429` with `Retry-After`) — token rotation lost means the supplier reconnects, so the plan keeps the last known stock and marks it stale rather than zeroing it, and bounds polling below the limit; Shopify `inventory_levels/update` webhooks (HMAC-SHA256, retries over 48 h, out-of-order delivery, no history) — the plan verifies the signature, orders by the payload's `updated_at`, ignores older updates, and states what happens after a missed event with no replay source; Northern Provisions' nightly SFTP CSV (missing 4 of 30 nights, truncated twice) — a missing or short file never zeroes stock, stale after a stated age, alert on absence, and the product-code mismatch the survey names for the nine Sage suppliers is flagged as an assumption in the spec that is false for them, not silently resolved. It replaces every vague quality line with a number, a method, and a source: stock shown within five minutes of a change at the source for polled and pushed systems, measured as source `updated_at` to `stock_updated_at` from a sync-run ledger and shown in Grafana; a nightly file within 26 hours; 99% of sync runs succeeding per supplier per week; outbound calls to any supplier under 50 per minute per token; catalogue p95 under 400 ms — and calls out SC-002 ('never stale') as impossible as written for a nightly feed, replacing it with a maximum age plus an 'as of' timestamp on the catalogue, flagged to the owner. The 500-connected-suppliers figure is treated as an unsourced planning assumption, carried as a capacity assumption to confirm, not a constraint. It classifies the hosting notes: the £300 monthly cap (Tom's e-mail) and the static egress IP with ten working days' notice (Northern Provisions' IT) are constraints with sources; 'ops would rather not add a second worker' is a preference, and the plan checks it against the cap (a second machine at £14 fits) rather than treating it as a boundary. Constraints become provisioning: a public webhook route on the `api` app with a per-shop secret; the worker's egress IP preserved (or the notice period scheduled) for the SFTP host; a place for per-supplier credentials, which no ruling covers (AX-013's note) — weighed across at least two real options (an encrypted column under the app key in PostgreSQL, Fly secrets, a vault) against the one-datastore principle and the residency rule; worker capacity for polling 38 suppliers under the limit; alerts on sync lag and on a missing nightly file (AX-012 has none of these). It surfaces what the spec omits by reading the store's own triggers: AX-010's caching trigger fires (the catalogue becomes a read-heavy surface — a decision on caching stock reads, with the staleness bound), AX-011's rate-limiting trigger fires on the first documented limit (outbound to Lightspeed; inbound webhook bursts), the override in FR-003 needs an audit record even though AX-008 excludes stock today, and sync-run logs need a retention period. It rejects the spec's 'stock levels are not sensitive': per-supplier OAuth tokens and the SFTP credential are Restricted, the stock and supplier codes Confidential commercial data under the counterparty principle, and a supplier's stock never appears in logs. Requirements are stated as what the system must achieve (stock reflected within the target; an out-of-stock product not addable), not as a queue job; each traces to its FR or SC; the decisions on where stock lives (columns on `Product` versus a stock-level table with history) and the polling interval are weighed against alternatives with the trade-off stated. The plan stops for the owner on SC-002, the Sage code mapping, and the credential-store ruling, naming a default for each.
assertions: plan maps Lightspeed, Shopify, and the SFTP feed as integration points with version, endpoints, limits, and concrete failure modes and fallbacks (keep last known stock and mark stale; never zero on a missing or short file; ignore out-of-order webhook updates), and asks the which-version / which-endpoint / timeout / retry questions of each

plan replaces near-real-time, reliable, don't-hammer, and 'never stale' with numeric targets, measurement methods, and sources, and flags SC-002 as impossible for a nightly feed rather than carrying it

plan classifies the £300 cap and the egress-IP notice as sourced constraints and the second-worker reluctance as a preference, treats the 500-supplier figure as an unsourced assumption, and traces the constraints to provisioning items (webhook ingress, egress IP, a credential store weighed against alternatives, worker capacity, sync alerts)

plan surfaces caching and rate limiting from the store's own not-now triggers, audit for the manual override, and log retention, rejects 'stock is not sensitive' by classifying credentials Restricted and stock Confidential, and flags the Sage product-code mismatch as a false assumption
note: Boundaries and targets golden. Plants, all visible: four vague quality lines and an impossible success criterion (SC-002 against a nightly CSV); three integration surfaces with documented limits and documented failure history; an assumption the survey contradicts (product ids match — not for the nine Sage suppliers); a sensitivity claim to reject (stock not sensitive — while OAuth tokens and an SFTP credential must be held and no per-tenant credential store exists, AX-013); two sourced constraints beside one preference in the hosting notes; two store triggers (AX-010 caching, AX-011 rate limiting) that this feature fires; and an audit exclusion (AX-008) that FR-003's override crosses. The unsourced 500-supplier figure is a light temptation for the constraints-without-sources claim; the pressure golden carries the strong one.
